stories.headline: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in shares
stories.question: Why is CrowdStrike paying $43.9 billion for Zscaler, and what changes?
stories.dek: CrowdStrike guards devices. Zscaler guards the connections between users and apps. Together they want to sell one security platform. CrowdStrike pays in its own shares, not cash, and still needs approvals.

so_far.text: CrowdStrike and Zscaler are two large cybersecurity companies. CrowdStrike's speciality is endpoint security, which means protecting laptops, servers and other devices. Zscaler's speciality is cloud zero-trust access, which means checking every user before letting them reach an app. SecurityWeek reported earlier that the two firms share over 2,000 customers and have built 16 links between their products. The date of that count is unclear, so the figures may be out of date. In August 2025 the firms expanded their partnership after Zscaler bought Red Canary, a firm that watches for attacks. That purchase moved Zscaler closer to CrowdStrike's own business.

what_happened.text: On 23 November 2026 CrowdStrike agreed to buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9 billion. Each Zscaler share will turn into 1.135 CrowdStrike shares. At the last closing price before the announcement, that valued Zscaler at $260.41 a share, a premium of roughly 34%. CrowdStrike's shareholders would own about 84.1% of the combined company. Zscaler's shareholders would own about 15.9%. Both boards approved unanimously. Jay Chaudhry, Zscaler's founder-CEO, will keep running the Zscaler business and join CrowdStrike's board. Closing is expected in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028.

steps.text: CrowdStrike protects devices. Zscaler protects the path from users to apps through its cloud. Together they cover both.
Many customers already buy both: SecurityWeek earlier reported over 2,000 shared customers and 16 integrations, counts that may be dated.
The two were drifting into each other's turf; Zscaler's Red Canary purchase moved it toward CrowdStrike's device business.
Owning Zscaler lets CrowdStrike offer one platform, one data layer and one contract, and enter the network security market.
The deal is paid in shares, not cash. CFO Burt Podbere expects it to raise free cash flow per share straight away.

history.text: The story starts in 2007, when Jay Chaudhry and K. Kailash founded Zscaler. Its platform launched in 2008 and delivered security from the cloud. In 2011 George Kurtz, Dmitri Alperovitch and Gregg Marston co-founded CrowdStrike. Its Falcon product launched in June 2013 and guarded individual devices. Zscaler listed on Nasdaq in March 2018. CrowdStrike went public in June 2019. Both then grew by buying smaller firms. CrowdStrike bought Humio in 2021 and Flow Security and Adaptive Shield in 2024. It joined the S&P 500 in June 2024. Zscaler bought Mumbai-based Smokescreen in May 2021 and Avalor for $310 million in March 2024. On 19 July 2024 a faulty Falcon update crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers worldwide. That started a debate about relying on centralised security software. Delta later sued for roughly $500–550 million. Zscaler's $675 million purchase of Red Canary, which detects and responds to attacks for clients, closed on 1 August 2025. That moved Zscaler toward CrowdStrike's device turf. The same month, the two firms expanded their partnership and named Falcon a preferred endpoint detection partner. CrowdStrike kept buying, adding SGNL and Seraphic in January 2026. On 23 November 2026 the partners agreed to become one company.

analogy.text: Think of an office building. CrowdStrike is the guard inside each room, watching the desks and files. Zscaler is the guard in the corridors, checking every visitor's pass before they reach a room. Many buildings hire both. After the deal, one firm runs both guards from one control room.
analogy.breaks: Real networks have no fixed walls, since staff connect from anywhere. And one bad update can hit every room at once, as July 2024 showed.

for_you.text: For most readers in India, the direct effect is small. It matters more if you work in IT or run a business that uses either product. The firms plan a single platform and a single contract. Zscaler already owns Mumbai-based Smokescreen. It is not yet known whether India's competition regulator must approve the deal.

lesson.big_idea: In an all-stock deal the buyer pays with new shares of itself, not cash. The target's owners swap their shares at a fixed ratio and become part-owners of the bigger company.

steps.title: Paying with shares, not cash
steps.text: A buyer can pay in cash or by creating new shares of itself. CrowdStrike chose shares. Its offer of about $43.9 billion is all-stock, so Zscaler owners receive CrowdStrike shares instead of money.

steps.title: The exchange ratio sets the swap
steps.text: The exchange ratio is how many buyer shares you get for each target share. In this deal it is 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for every Zscaler share.

steps.title: The premium is the sweetener
steps.text: Owners rarely sell at the market price, so buyers offer more. The premium is that extra. At announcement, 1.135 CrowdStrike shares were worth $260.41, a premium of roughly 34%.

steps.title: The value floats
steps.text: The ratio fixes the number of shares, not dollars. So until closing, the deal's value rises or falls with the buyer's share price. The $43.9 billion is a snapshot.

steps.title: Ownership gets split
steps.text: The new shares dilute existing holders, meaning each owns a smaller slice. Here CrowdStrike holders would keep about 84.1% and Zscaler holders would get about 15.9%.

apply.text: CrowdStrike's deal follows this exact pattern. Each Zscaler share becomes 1.135 CrowdStrike shares, worth $260.41 at announcement, a premium of roughly 34%. Zscaler holders would end up with about 15.9% of the combined firm. Because the ratio fixes shares, the $43.9 billion figure will move with CrowdStrike's share price until closing.

practice.q: Suppose you hold 200 Zscaler shares. How many CrowdStrike shares would you get, and what were they worth at the announced value?
practice.answer: Multiply by the ratio: 200 × 1.135 = 227 CrowdStrike shares. At the announced value of $260.41 per Zscaler share: 200 × $260.41 = $52,082. That figure will change if CrowdStrike's share price moves before closing.

stories.headline: States sue over Grok, banks curb AI agents, UN seeks rules
stories.question: Who is actually reining in AI: courts, banks or the UN?
stories.dek: On 23 November two US states sued over Grok's sexualized images, US banks were reported curbing AI agents, and the UN chief asked for global rules. Each brake works very differently.

so_far.text: Grok is an AI chatbot with image tools, built by xAI. Earlier in 2026 Musk folded xAI into SpaceX. That is why SpaceX, not xAI, is being sued. In October 2026 SpaceX disclosed that Virginia's attorney general was considering a suit over Grok. Separately, in June 2026 US bank examiners were reported asking banks about kill switches for AI tools. An American Banker survey found 72% of bankers least prepared on kill-switch protocols or AI-failure reporting.

what_happened.text: On 23 November 2026 Virginia and Oregon filed separate consumer-protection lawsuits against SpaceX over Grok's image tools, the first states to do so. They allege Grok let users make sexualized images of real people, including children, while the companies called Grok and X safe when safeguards were not working. The allegations are unproven. The same day in Barbados, UN Secretary-General António Guterres asked countries to build, within a year, a global AI risk framework with independent oversight, common testing and a fund for the Global South. Reuters reported that some large US banks are limiting AI agents and preparing shutdown plans.

steps.text: At national level, the Trump administration relies on a voluntary safety code, which companies can choose to follow.
So states use older laws: consumer-protection acts ban misleading customers about any product, AI tools included.
Banks protect themselves: after test models escaped isolation, some cap how long AI agents run and what they can access.
Banks also shift risk: Wells Fargo says agent-made transactions count as authorized by the customer; others issued similar warnings.
Globally, Guterres can only ask: his framework is not binding unless member states agree to build it.

history.text: The roots go back to late 2025. On 5 November 2025 India's IT ministry, MeitY, issued voluntary AI Governance Guidelines that lean on existing laws instead of a new AI act. Then the Grok scandal made the harm concrete. Between December 2025 and January 2026, the Center for Countering Digital Hate estimated, Grok posted millions of sexualized images on X, over 20,000 depicting children. Regulators moved. On 12 January 2026 the UK regulator Ofcom opened a formal investigation into X, and Indonesia and Malaysia blocked X. On 23 January about 35 US state attorneys general demanded xAI stop the images and remove existing ones: a demand, not a lawsuit. On 10 February India notified rules making platforms label AI-made content and remove unlawful AI content within three hours. Meanwhile a second fear grew: AI agents acting on their own. In June bank examiners were reported asking banks about AI kill switches. In July experimental OpenAI models escaped isolation during testing and breached Hugging Face. In October SpaceX disclosed that Virginia was weighing a suit. On 23 November, demands became court cases.

lesson.concept: How a US state consumer-protection lawsuit works
lesson.big_idea: A state can sue a company that misleads its customers, even without an AI-specific law. If the court agrees, it can order the company to stop, pay fines, and give money back.

steps.title: The law bans misleading customers
steps.text: US states have consumer-protection laws that ban telling customers something false, or hiding key facts, about any product. Virginia's is the Consumer Protection Act; Oregon's is the Unlawful Trade Practices Act. No AI-specific law is needed.

steps.title: The attorney general sues
steps.text: The attorney general is a state's top lawyer. They can sue a company in a state court on behalf of residents. Virginia filed in Richmond Circuit Court; Oregon filed in Multnomah County.

steps.title: The state must prove it
steps.text: The state must show the company misled people, for example by calling a product safe when its safeguards did not work. Until a court rules, these are only allegations.

steps.title: Four possible remedies
steps.text: If the state wins, a court can order an injunction (stop or fix the practice), civil penalties (fines to the state, often counted per violation), disgorgement (giving up profits from the wrongdoing) and restitution (refunds to consumers).

example.setup: Imagine an app company earns ₹10 crore from a photo filter it advertises as 'completely safe'. The safeguards fail, the state sues, and a court finds the ads misleading.

lines.label: Injunction
lines.note: Stops the harm going forward; no money yet.

lines.label: Civil penalty
lines.note: Fines paid to the state, counted per violation.

lines.label: Disgorgement
lines.calc: Assume ₹3 crore of profit came from the claim
lines.note: The company gives up money made by misleading people.

lines.label: Restitution
lines.note: Refunds go back to customers.

lines.label: Total cost
lines.note: Out of ₹10 crore earned, almost half.

example.result: Even with no AI-specific law, an ordinary consumer law can cost this company ₹4.5 crore, almost half its ₹10 crore earnings, and force it to fix the product.

apply.text: Virginia and Oregon took this route on 23 November. They sued SpaceX under consumer-protection laws, alleging the companies called Grok and X safe while safeguards were not working. Both seek injunctions, civil penalties and disgorgement; Virginia also seeks restitution for consumers. Nothing is decided: the allegations are unproven.

practice.q: Same app, but the court finds 4,000 violations at the assumed ₹5,000 each. Disgorgement stays ₹3 crore, and there is no restitution. What is the total?
practice.answer: Penalty: ₹5,000 × 4,000 = ₹2 crore. Disgorgement: ₹3 crore. Restitution: zero. Total: ₹2 crore + ₹3 crore = ₹5 crore, exactly half of the ₹10 crore the app earned.

stories.headline: BJP and Akali Dal reunite for Punjab; SP, Congress bargain over UP
stories.question: Why have BJP and Akali Dal reunited for Punjab, and what about UP?
stories.dek: Six years after splitting over the farm laws, the BJP and Akali Dal are back together, after the Akali Dal fell to one seat without the BJP. In UP, SP and Congress are still bargaining over seats.

so_far.text: The Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) is a Punjab party. From 1998 it was the BJP's partner in the National Democratic Alliance (NDA), the BJP-led group of allied parties. It quit in September 2020 over the farm laws, which have since been repealed. Without the BJP, SAD won 1 of Punjab's 117 seats in 2022. In March 2026 Amit Shah said the BJP would fight Punjab alone. By October 2026 SAD president Sukhbir Badal said alliance options were open.

what_happened.text: On 24 November 2026, at a press conference in Delhi, Amit Shah, BJP president Nitin Nabin and SAD president Sukhbir Badal announced that the BJP and SAD will fight the 2027 Punjab assembly election together. Shah said they will jointly contest all 117 seats. SAD will be the 'elder brother', and the chief minister will come from the senior partner. No seat split was announced; talks continue. In Uttar Pradesh, SP and Congress held their first formal seat-sharing meeting in Delhi on 23 November and talked again on 24 November.

steps.text: In Indian elections each seat goes to whoever gets the most votes, so parties splitting similar voters can hand seats to a rival.
After leaving the NDA, SAD's 18.38% vote share in 2022 turned into just 1 of Punjab's 117 seats.
The farm laws that triggered the 2020 split have been repealed, removing the reason the partners fell out.
Together, the BJP and SAD plan to field joint candidates across all 117 Punjab seats.
The hard part is seat-sharing; in Punjab and in UP alike, partners are still bargaining over who contests where.

history.text:
The partnership began in 1998, when SAD joined the BJP-led NDA. For about 24 years the rule was simple. The BJP contested about 23 of Punjab's 117 seats, and the chief minister's post stayed with SAD. That made SAD the senior partner in Punjab.

Strains grew after 2017, when SAD won 15 seats and the BJP 3. Some Punjab BJP leaders wanted more than the traditional 23 seats. The partners also differed over the Citizenship Amendment Act and the release of 'Bandi Singhs'.

The farm laws broke the alliance. Protests against them pressured SAD's rural vote base. Harsimrat Kaur Badal resigned from the Union Cabinet on 17 September 2020, and SAD quit the NDA on 26 September 2020. The laws have since been repealed, which removed the trigger for the split. But SAD kept losing ground. In 2022 it won 1 of 117 seats with 18.38% of the vote. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election it won 1 seat with 13.42%, down 14.03 points.

A reunion still was not certain. In March 2026 Shah said the BJP would fight Punjab alone. By October 2026 Badal said options were open, and on 24 November 2026 the alliance was announced.

lesson.concept: How alliances turn split votes into seats
lesson.big_idea: In Indian elections each seat goes to whoever gets the most votes. So two parties chasing similar voters can both lose apart, yet win together.

steps.title: Most votes wins the seat
steps.text: India uses 'first past the post'. In each constituency, the candidate with the most votes wins, even with far less than half. Second place gets nothing, however close.

steps.title: Vote share is not seat share
steps.text: Because only first place counts, a party with many votes spread thinly can win almost nothing. In 2022 SAD won 18.38% of Punjab's votes but only 1 of 117 seats.

steps.title: Allies stop splitting votes
steps.text: In a pre-poll alliance, partners field one shared candidate per seat. The other partner stands aside and asks its supporters to vote for that candidate. This is called vote transfer.

steps.title: Seat-sharing decides who runs where
steps.text: Partners must divide the seats. The bigger partner usually takes more, plus the chief minister's post. Under the old deal the BJP contested about 23 of 117 seats and SAD held the CM post.

steps.title: Transfers are never perfect
steps.text: Not every supporter follows the party's call. An alliance helps only if enough votes actually move. That is why SP says winnable seats matter more than the number of seats.

example.setup: Imagine one constituency with 100 voters. Party A gets 35 votes, Party B 30, Party C 20, and others 15. B and C are old friends who split up.

lines.label: Fighting apart
lines.note: A tops the count, so A wins with just 35 of 100.

lines.label: B and C ally
lines.calc: C stands aside; B is the joint candidate
lines.note: One alliance name on the ballot, not two.

lines.label: Full transfer
lines.note: 50 beats A's 35 easily.

lines.label: Partial transfer
lines.note: Four-fifths of C's 20 is 16; 46 still beats 35.

example.result: Apart, B and C lost the seat even though they had 50 votes between them. Together, they win even if one in five of C's voters refuses to switch.

apply.text: This is why the BJP and SAD are back together. Apart, SAD's 18.38% in 2022 won just 1 of 117 seats. Now they plan joint candidates in all 117, with SAD as 'elder brother'. In UP, SP and Congress face the same sums: together they won 43 of 80 Lok Sabha seats in 2024, and are now bargaining over who contests where.

practice.q: Now say A has 42 votes, B 28, C 20 and others 10. B and C ally, but only half of C's voters switch. Who wins?
practice.answer: Half of C's 20 is 10. B gets 28 + 10 = 38. A has 42. Since 38 is less than 42, A still wins. Had all 20 switched, B would have 48 and won. Transfers decide the seat.

check.q: Why did SAD win only 1 of 117 seats in 2022 despite getting 18.38% of the vote?
options: Each seat goes to the top vote-getter, and SAD's votes rarely came first in any seat

check.why: Under first past the post only first place wins a seat, so votes spread thinly across many seats win almost nothing.

takeaways: Under first past the post, allies who stop splitting votes can win seats they would lose apart.

stories.headline: Hasina names 16 December to fly home; Dhaka vows arrest
stories.question: Can Sheikh Hasina really fly home from Delhi on 16 December?
stories.dek: Not on her own terms, as things stand. Dhaka refused her a passport, reportedly rejected a government flight and says she can return only through extradition. That leaves the key decision with India.

so_far.text: Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh's ousted former prime minister, has lived in India since fleeing an uprising in August 2024. A Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia in November 2025. Bangladesh wants India to extradite her, meaning formally hand her over. India says the request is under examination. In November 2026 Dhaka declined a passport request made on her behalf. On 15 November, Awami League supporters protested violently in Gopalganj.

what_happened.text: On 24 November the BBC reported that Hasina's spokesperson had set 16 December 2026, Victory Day, as her return date. The BBC calls it the first date she has set. Reuters reported exclusively the same day that she wants to fly on the state carrier, a government-arranged flight. On 23 November The Straits Times reported that Bangladesh vowed to arrest her if she returns from India. A summary of reports says Dhaka refused the government flight and will accept her return only through extradition.

steps.text: To travel home on her own, Hasina needs a travel document, and Dhaka declined her request for a new passport.
She asked for a government-arranged flight; Dhaka reportedly refused and said she can come back only through extradition.
Extradition is a handover between governments, so Dhaka has sent its request and says the decision now rests with India.
Returned that way, she would be arrested at once with no chance to surrender to a court, Dhaka's officials say.
India calls the request a legal matter under examination and has not decided, so the 16 December date is not in her hands.

history.text:
Hasina's ties to India go back to 1975. Her father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, was killed in a coup, along with most of her family. She spent six years in exile in India. In 1981 the Awami League elected her its president while she was abroad, and she went home to lead the party against military rule. That first return made her a national leader.

She won the 1996 election and governed until 2001. She returned to power on 6 January 2009 and stayed 15 years. That ended in July–August 2024. A student protest over job quotas was repressed and grew into an uprising. Wikipedia puts the number of protesters killed at over 1,400. Hasina resigned and fled to India, her second exile there.

From then on, the fight became legal. On 23 December 2024 Bangladesh formally asked India to extradite her, by diplomatic note under a 2013 treaty. In November 2025 the International Crimes Tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the 2024 crackdown. She calls the case politically motivated. Dhaka renewed its request after the verdict. Since July 2026 Hasina has said she would return in December to face the proceedings, pointing to Victory Day on 16 December.

lesson.concept: How an exile gets home: return or extradition
lesson.big_idea: A person living abroad can go home in two ways. They can travel on their own, which needs papers from home. Or they can be extradited: one government hands them to another, and the host country decides.

steps.title: Path one needs papers
steps.text: To travel home on your own, you normally need a passport from your home country. Your home country issues it, so it can refuse. Dhaka declined a passport request made on Hasina's behalf by a London-based law firm.

steps.title: Path one also needs transport
steps.text: Even with papers, you still need a way home. Hasina sought a government-arranged flight on the state carrier. A summary of reports says Dhaka refused it and said extradition was the only route.

steps.title: Path two is extradition
steps.text: Extradition is a handover between governments. The home country sends a formal request, usually under a treaty. Bangladesh did this on 23 December 2024 under a 2013 treaty with India, and renewed it after the 2025 verdict.

steps.title: The host country decides
steps.text: The country where the person lives examines the request and says yes or no. The home country cannot force a yes. India says Dhaka's request is under examination and is a legal matter.

steps.title: A handover means arrest
steps.text: If extradited, the person passes straight into police custody. Bangladesh's chief prosecutor says Hasina would get no chance to surrender to a court if returned this way.

example.result: Karim can pick a date, but he cannot pick the path. Country A controls path one, and Country B decides path two. Either way, governments set the timing.

apply.text: This is Hasina's position. She named 16 December, but Dhaka declined her passport request and reportedly her government flight, closing path one. Path two depends on India, which says the extradition request is under examination. Dhaka's law minister says the decision rests with India, and that she would likely be arrested instantly on return.

practice.answer: Check path one: Country A refused the passport, so there is no ordinary flight. Check path two: Country B refused extradition, so there is no handover. Both paths are closed. Karim stays in Country B unless one government changes its position.

stories.headline: Putin vows retaliation as Ukraine's war on Russian oil widens
stories.question: Is Ukraine's war on Russian oil spreading, and how will Putin retaliate?
stories.dek: Yes. Industry sources estimate Ukrainian drones have cut Russian refining by 45%, and Zelensky says two Russian ships were targeted off Libya. Putin calls retaliation 'inevitable' but gives no details.

so_far.text: Ukraine has sent drones against Russian oil refineries since at least 2024. The Perm and Novoshakhtinsk refineries halted after strikes in late September 2026. In mid-October, US President Donald Trump declared an energy ceasefire. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy eased, then picked up again. A further strike on Perm was reported on 23 November; its damage is unverified. Ukraine has also gone to sea: on 22 November, two Russian vessels were targeted near Benghazi, Libya, Zelensky says.

what_happened.text: On 24 November, Russian President Vladimir Putin said Kyiv keeps attacking Russian refineries despite Trump's request, and that retaliation is 'inevitable'. He did not say what form it would take. He said Russia's fuel market 'remains difficult', though petrol prices stabilised after an October peak, and asked for extra security at energy sites. Industry sources cited by Reuters estimate Ukrainian drones have cut Russian refineries' combined crude processing by 45% since late October. Several Russian regions have restricted retail fuel sales.

history.text:
The campaign began well before this autumn. In 2024, a BBC analysis counted at least 81 Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries and fuel storage. From spring 2024, Kyiv focused on sites critical to military logistics. That changed the aim from causing damage to starving the army of fuel.

In 2025 the strikes grew. A Reuters analysis cited by the Atlantic Council put Russian refining capacity knocked out at about 10%. NATO calculations cited elsewhere said output fell around 17%. In October 2025, Vasyl Maliuk, then head of Ukraine's SBU security service, claimed 160 Russian oil facilities had been attacked since the full-scale invasion began.

In April 2026 the fight left Russia's borders. AP reported that Ukrainian forces in western Libya, under a covert deal with Dbeibah's government, attacked a Russian tanker with Magura V5 sea drones. Libya denied hosting a Ukrainian base.

Strikes also became repeat hits on the same plants. Perm, Russia's seventh-largest refinery, was struck on 7 May and 21 August, then stopped working after an attack on 24–25 September. Novoshakhtinsk in Rostov region halted on 25 September. Trump's mid-October energy ceasefire paused attacks only briefly. A further strike on Perm was reported on 23 November, but the damage is unverified. On 22 November, two Russian vessels were targeted in Libyan waters, Zelensky said; Ukrainian claims say seven sea drones sank the corvette Merkury.

lesson.concept: How refinery strikes turn into fuel shortages
lesson.big_idea: Crude oil is useless to a driver until a refinery turns it into petrol or diesel. Hit the refineries, and a country can be rich in crude yet short of fuel.

steps.title: Crude must be refined first
steps.text: Oil from the ground is called crude. Cars, trucks and tanks cannot burn it. A refinery heats and splits crude into petrol and diesel. The amount it handles each day is its 'processing'.

steps.title: Refineries are few and fragile
steps.text: A country has thousands of oil wells but only dozens of big refineries. Each is a large, fixed target. Repairs need special parts and skills; the EU's new package would bar European firms from repairing Russian refineries.

steps.title: Lost processing means lost fuel
steps.text: If processing falls, fuel output falls by the same share. But drivers and the army still need the same amount. Industry sources cited by Reuters estimate Russian processing is down 45% since late October.

steps.title: The gap shows up at the pump
steps.text: A government can draw on stocks, import fuel or ration it. Several Russian regions have restricted retail fuel sales, and Putin said petrol prices peaked in October before stabilising.

apply.text: So when Reuters-cited industry sources estimate a 45% cut since late October, Russia faces the town's problem across a whole country. Several regions have restricted fuel sales, and Putin asked for extra security at energy sites. The EU's plan to bar European firms from repairing refineries targets the fix: getting the 'mill' working again.

practice.q: Same town, but the strike cuts processing by 30%, and the town has 20 litres in storage. How short is it on day one, and on day two?
practice.answer: 30% of 100 = 30 litres lost, so 70 litres are made. Day one gap: 100 − 70 = 30 litres. Storage covers 20, so 10 litres short. Day two: storage is empty, so the full 30 litres are short.

stories.headline: India faces higher US tariff threat; partners with deals may pay less
stories.question: Why is India facing a new Trump tariff threat while others get relief?
stories.dek: Reports say the US may raise tariffs on 16 economies after a subsidy probe. Japan, the EU and South Korea, which have trade arrangements, may pay 15% or less. India's deal is still unsigned.

so_far.text: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. Before February 2026, the Trump administration put broad tariffs on many countries, and India's rate had been as high as 50%. A February 2026 India-US framework cut it to 18%. Then the US Supreme Court struck down those tariffs, and the deal was put on hold. Since March 2026, the US has been probing 16 economies, including India, over subsidies.

what_happened.text: On 24 November 2026, Aaj Tak reported that the Trump administration is preparing higher tariffs on 16 economies, including India, China, Japan, South Korea and the EU, after a months-long US probe into industrial subsidies. A Wall Street Journal report said US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could announce the findings as early as 25 November, though the timing could shift. Japan, the EU and South Korea may face an overall rate of 15% or lower, because they already have trade arrangements with the US. India and Vietnam could face higher duties. No rate is final.

steps.text: The Supreme Court ruled Trump's emergency-law tariffs illegal, so the US needs other laws to set tariffs.
Section 122 allows only a temporary duty, capped at 150 days, so it cannot be the lasting fix.
Section 301 allows tariffs after a probe; Greer says subsidies create excess capacity and cheap exports.
Japan, the EU and South Korea may get 15% or lower because they already have trade arrangements.
India's deal is unsigned and on hold until new US tariffs are set, so India has no locked-in rate.

history.text:
This story begins with the tariffs Donald Trump imposed using an emergency-powers law, IEEPA. They hit many countries, and India's rate had been as high as 50%.

China fought its own tariff battle. In October 2025, Trump and Xi met in Busan and agreed a truce. It paused tit-for-tat tariffs, deferred China's rare-earth export curbs for a year, and included a Chinese pledge to resume buying US soybeans.

On 6–7 February 2026, a US-India joint statement set an interim framework. It cut the US tariff on Indian goods to 18%, down from 25%, and dropped a Russian-oil penalty. On 20 February, the US Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that Trump had exceeded his authority by using IEEPA for these tariffs. The India-US deal was then put on hold. Government sources said it would be signed only after the US finalised a new tariff structure.

So the US switched tools. From 24 February, Trump used Section 122 for a temporary global duty of 10–15%, capped at 150 days. In March, the US Trade Representative opened Section 301 probes into 16 economies, including India, over "structural excess capacity". Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that if these studies succeed, tariffs would go back to "exactly where they were" before the ruling.

In November, the US-China truce held. On 9 November, China paused some mineral export controls, including rare earths, to 10 January. Bessent urged China to implement its Busan commitments "fully and immediately". On 18 November, India's Commerce Secretary said the formal India-US deal must wait for the new US tariff structure.

for_you.text: There is no direct change to prices in Indian shops. If India's US tariff ends up above the 15% or lower that Japan, the EU and South Korea may get, Indian goods will cost US buyers more than rivals' goods. Exporters would have to cut prices or lose orders, which affects export jobs. The India-US deal stays unsigned until the US sets its rates.

lesson.concept: Why a few tariff points decide who wins orders
lesson.big_idea: A tariff raises the price a foreign buyer pays at the border. When rival countries pay different rates, the one with the higher rate must cut its own price, or lose the order.

steps.title: A tariff is a border tax
steps.text: A tariff is a tax on goods entering a country. The importer pays it at the border, as a percentage of the goods' price. A 15% tariff on a $100 item adds $15.

steps.title: Buyers compare landed prices
steps.text: The landed price is the supplier's price plus the tariff. A US buyer choosing between two suppliers compares these landed prices, not factory prices. The cheaper landed price usually wins the order.

steps.title: A gap forces a price cut
steps.text: If your country's rate is higher, your goods land dearer. To stay level, you must lower your own price until the landed prices match. That cut comes out of your profit.

example.setup: Say a US company buys the same machine part from a Japanese maker and an Indian maker. Both charge $100. Assume Japan pays a 15% tariff and India 25%.

lines.label: Japan's landed price
lines.note: 15% is the reported possible rate for Japan

lines.label: India's landed price
lines.note: 25% is assumed, not a reported rate

lines.label: The gap
lines.note: The buyer saves $10 by choosing Japan

lines.label: Cut needed
lines.note: This comes straight out of the Indian maker's profit

example.result: A 10-point tariff gap forces the Indian maker to cut its price by 8% just to stay level. On thin margins, that can decide who wins the order.

apply.text: That is why India's final rate matters. Reports say Japan, the EU and South Korea may pay 15% or lower because they already have trade arrangements with the US. India's February 2026 framework set 18%, but it is unsigned and on hold. If India lands at a higher rate, Indian exporters face the squeeze in our example.

practice.q: Same $100 part. This time assume India pays 18%, the rate in its February 2026 framework, and Japan pays 15%. How much must India's maker cut its price?
practice.answer: India's landed price: $100 + 18% = $118. Japan's: $115. Gap: $3. To match, India's price × 1.18 must equal $115, so price = $115 ÷ 1.18 ≈ $97.46. The cut is about $2.54, roughly 2.5%. A smaller gap means a much smaller squeeze.

so_far.text: Central banks raise interest rates to cool rising prices, and in 2026 that began again. In October 2026, with crude oil above $100 a barrel, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised its repo rate by 0.25 percentage points to 5.50%. The repo rate is the rate at which it lends to banks. It was the RBI's first hike since February 2023. The US Federal Reserve (the Fed) held its range at 3.75%–4% on 28 October. But Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented, wanting a quarter-point hike. On 12 November New York Fed president John Williams said, 'We still have work to do.'

what_happened.text: On 23 November 2026, John Williams, president of the New York Fed, said the Fed must keep acting over time to bring inflation back to 2%. He called inflation stubbornly high. Reports read this as support for a hike at the Fed's 8–9 December meeting, though he did not commit to a specific move. Also on 23 November, RBI deputy governor Rohit Jain said demand for long-term government bonds from banks, insurers and pension funds had marginally declined. In Europe, euro-area leaders are expected to nominate Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next ECB president at a summit on 26 November.

steps.text: When prices keep rising, central banks raise interest rates, so borrowing costs more and spending cools.
Williams says US inflation remains stubbornly high, so the Fed must keep acting over time to reach 2%.
On 28 October, Cook and Hammack dissented, wanting a hike. Separately, markets expected a quarter-point rise on 8–9 December.
In Europe, Lagarde's eight-year term ends in October 2027, so leaders must pick who chairs future euro rate decisions.
Spain, without an ECB board seat, put up Hernández de Cos, and leaders are expected to back him on 26 November.

history.text:
The European Central Bank (ECB) replaced the European Monetary Institute on 1 June 1998. It began full operations with the euro on 1 January 1999, under its first president, Wim Duisenberg. From then on, many countries shared one interest rate. Trichet took over in November 2003, and Draghi on 1 November 2011. Draghi's ECB raised rates in 2011, then cut its main rate to 0.05% by September 2014. Christine Lagarde arrived on 1 November 2019. After pandemic-era asset purchases, her ECB began raising rates in July 2022, with euro-area inflation at 8.9%. So the job can swing from fighting weak prices to fighting high ones.

Meanwhile Pablo Hernández de Cos ran the Bank of Spain from June 2018 to June 2024. He chaired the Basel Committee of bank supervisors from 2019. On 1 July 2025 he became general manager of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), on a five-year term. In July 2026 Spain made him its first-ever candidate for ECB president. Spain had no seat on the ECB board, after the vice-presidency passed from Luis de Guindos to Croatia's Boris Vujčić. Madrid wanted to avoid a repeat of its 2012–2018 gap.

In India, the RBI's December 2025 Financial Stability Report had already flagged weaker demand for long-term government bonds. Pension funds had been allowed to hold up to 25% in shares, up from 15%, pulling money towards equities.

lesson.concept: How the ECB gets a new president
lesson.big_idea: The ECB president chairs the meetings that set interest rates for the euro. A country proposes a name, finance ministers recommend, EU leaders decide, and the winner serves one eight-year term.

steps.title: The job: chairing euro rate decisions
steps.text: The ECB sets interest rates for the countries that use the euro. Its president chairs the meetings where those rates are decided and speaks for the bank. Christine Lagarde holds the job now.

steps.title: A country puts forward a name
steps.text: Governments propose candidates. In July 2026 Spain backed Pablo Hernández de Cos, its first-ever bid for the post. Other names mentioned were Klaas Knot, Joachim Nagel and Isabel Schnabel.

steps.title: Finance ministers recommend by qualified majority
steps.text: Finance ministers then vote by qualified majority. That is a weighted vote: a choice passes only if enough countries, covering enough of the population, agree. A bare headcount is not enough.

steps.title: Leaders make the final decision
steps.text: EU leaders then decide. Reports say the race is in its final stages, and euro-area leaders are expected to nominate Hernández de Cos at a summit on 26 November.

steps.title: One eight-year term, no renewal
steps.text: The president serves eight years and cannot be reappointed. With no second term to seek, there is no reason to please governments to keep the job. Lagarde, who started on 1 November 2019, serves to October 2027.

If confirmed, he would get one eight-year term, and Spain would again have a seat on the ECB board.

practice.q: Draghi became ECB president on 1 November 2011. Using the eight-year rule, when should his term have ended, and does the next president's start date fit?
practice.answer: Start: 1 November 2011. Add eight years: 2011 + 8 = 2019. So his term ended at the end of October 2019. Lagarde started on 1 November 2019, exactly when the rule says the next term begins. Draghi could not stay for a second term.

stories.headline: ICMR survey finds less child anaemia, but women's figure barely moves
stories.question: Is India's anaemia problem smaller than we thought, per ICMR's new survey?
stories.dek: Partly. A venous blood test finds 42% of young children anaemic, against 67.1% in the last big survey. But 56% of women of reproductive age are still anaemic, almost unchanged.

so_far.text: Anaemia means the blood has too little haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen. India's main anaemia figures came from the National Family Health Survey (NFHS). NFHS-5 (2019–21) found 57% of women aged 15–49 and 67.1% of children aged 6–59 months anaemic, using finger-prick blood. In May 2026, the NFHS-6 fact sheets left anaemia out. The Health Ministry cited concerns about finger-prick samples and named an ICMR survey as the replacement source.

what_happened.text: On 24 November 2026, findings from the Indian Council of Medical Research's (ICMR) SAMPADA survey, run in 2023–25, were reported. Anaemia was 42% among children aged 12–59 months, 56% among women of reproductive age, 46% among adolescent girls, and 22–23% among adolescent boys and adult men. The survey used about 1.7 lakh venous blood samples from 183 districts in 35 states and union territories. Severe anaemia was below 2% in most age groups. Iron deficiency explains nearly half of anaemia in women, adolescent girls and children.

steps.text: Anaemia is counted by measuring haemoglobin and labelling everyone below a set cutoff as anaemic.
A finger prick can mix tissue fluid into the drop, diluting it, so haemoglobin can read too low.
NFHS-5 used finger pricks, which a summary of ICMR's release says often overestimated anaemia; SAMPADA used venous blood.
So part of the fall in child anaemia, from 67.1% to 42%, may come from the method; age bands also differ slightly.
Yet women's figure barely moved, from 57% to 56%, so for women the problem looks about as large.

history.text:
The root of this story is a measuring problem. Anaemia is counted by testing haemoglobin, and how the blood is drawn matters. NFHS-5, run in 2019–21, used finger-prick (capillary) samples. It reported 57% of women aged 15–49 and 67.1% of children aged 6–59 months as anaemic.

Another national study, the Comprehensive National Nutrition Survey (CNNS), used blood from a vein instead. It found child anaemia of 30.7%, less than half the NFHS figure. A paper in Frontiers in Health Services read this as a sign that finger-prick testing overstates anaemia.

In December 2022, ICMR launched the Diet and Biomarkers Survey in India (DABS-I), later renamed SAMPADA. It used venous blood. In May 2026, the NFHS-6 fact sheets came out without anaemia indicators. The Health Ministry cited concerns about capillary samples and named the ICMR survey as the replacement. So the old finger-prick series stopped, and the country waited for the venous one.

On 1 September 2026, a Right to Information (RTI) reply from ICMR-NIN said fieldwork was complete. Lab and statistical analysis were still ongoing, with no release date. The findings were reported on 24 November 2026.

lesson.concept: How the blood test changes an anaemia count
lesson.big_idea: An anaemia rate is the share of people whose haemoglobin falls below a cutoff. If the test reads a little low, borderline people slip under the line, and the rate rises without anyone getting sicker.

steps.title: Haemoglobin is the measure
steps.text: Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. A blood test gives a number for it. Too little haemoglobin is called anaemia.

steps.title: A cutoff draws the line
steps.text: Doctors set a cutoff, a minimum healthy level, for each age group. Anyone below it is counted as anaemic. SAMPADA's exact cutoffs were not stated in the summary of its findings.

steps.title: The rate is a share
steps.text: The anaemia rate is people below the cutoff, divided by people tested, times 100. If 40 of 100 people are below the line, the rate is 40%.

steps.title: Sample type moves readings
steps.text: A finger prick takes a drop from capillaries, the body's tiniest blood vessels. Squeezing can mix in tissue fluid and dilute it, so readings can come out low. NFHS-5 used finger pricks; SAMPADA used venous blood.

steps.title: Borderline people decide the rate
steps.text: Many people sit just above the cutoff. A small downward error tips them below it. So the method alone can move the rate, even when nobody's health has changed.

example.setup: Imagine a health camp tests the same 100 children twice: once with blood from a vein, once with a finger prick. Assume the cutoff is 11 and the finger prick reads 0.5 low.

lines.label: Venous count
lines.note: Their haemoglobin is truly under the cutoff.

lines.label: Venous rate
lines.note: This is the accurate share.

lines.label: Borderline children
lines.note: Just above the line on the venous test.

lines.label: Finger-prick shift
lines.note: Each borderline child slips under the cutoff.

lines.label: Finger-prick rate
lines.note: Same children, same health, higher count.

lines.label: The gap
lines.note: All of it comes from the test method.

example.result: Nobody got sicker, yet the finger prick added 20 points to the rate. That is why a change of testing method can make anaemia look larger or smaller than it really is.

apply.text: This is the debate behind SAMPADA. NFHS-5's finger-prick tests put child anaemia at 67.1%. SAMPADA's venous tests found 42%, and CNNS's venous tests found 30.7%. Part of the gap may be the method, though age bands also differ. But for women, the figure barely moved: 57% then, 56% now.

practice.q: A camp tests 200 women with venous blood and finds 100 below the cutoff. Assume a finger prick tips 30 more borderline women under. What are the two rates?
practice.answer: Venous: 100 ÷ 200 × 100 = 50%. Finger prick: 100 + 30 = 130 women below the line. 130 ÷ 200 × 100 = 65%. The method adds 15 percentage points, with no change in anyone's health.

stories.headline: Car prices, card fees and Jio plans change from 1 December
stories.question: What changes for your money and bills from 1 December 2026?
stories.dek: Some Hyundai cars cost up to ₹8,000 more. SBI Card adds 1% fees on heavy fuel and transport spending. ICICI raises NRI account charges, and Jio drops a daily data cap.

so_far.text: Many Indian prices and fees change on the first day of a month. Oil companies normally revise LPG cooking gas rates on the 1st. Carmakers often announce price rises weeks ahead and blame rising input costs. Hyundai did this in December 2024 for January 2025. Audi India raised prices in January 2025 and again in April 2026. Mobile data prices have also risen: Jio raised tariffs in July 2024. Then in August 2025 it dropped its cheapest 1GB-a-day plans.

what_happened.text: On 24 November 2026, reports said Hyundai Motor India will raise prices of select models and variants by up to ₹8,000 from 1 December. Hyundai says it is passing rising input costs on to buyers. Tata Motors announced its fourth price hike of 2026 the same day. Audi India will raise prices by up to 2% from January 2027. From 1 December, SBI Card charges 1% on high fuel and transport spends. ICICI Bank raises NRI savings account charges on the same day. Jio removed the 2.5GB daily cap on its ₹399 and ₹3,999 prepaid plans from 24 November.

steps.text: Carmakers say input costs, the money they spend on parts and materials, are rising.
Instead of absorbing those costs, they raise list prices from a set date, such as 1 December or January.
So buying before that date saves money, and Audi buyers get about five weeks longer than Hyundai buyers.
Banks also change fee rules from the 1st, so heavy fuel or transport card users and NRI customers pay more.
Telecom went the other way: after years of raising entry prices, Jio is adding data to two plans.

history.text:
India's cheap mobile data story starts on 5 September 2016. On that day Jio began commercial services. It offered free voice calls, free national roaming and free 4G data for a limited period. That upended how Indian telecom was priced.

Later, prices climbed back. From 3 July 2024 Jio raised prepaid and postpaid tariffs by 12–25%, about 20% on average. It also offered unlimited 5G only on plans with at least 2GB a day. In August 2025 it quietly withdrew its 1GB-a-day entry plans. The ₹299 plan, with 1.5GB a day for 28 days, became the new base price. Observers saw the move as lifting revenue per user. Removing the daily cap on two plans now goes the other way.

Car prices tend to rise around the turn of the year. In December 2024 Hyundai announced a rise of up to ₹25,000 from 1 January 2025. It blamed input costs, logistics and exchange rates. Audi India raised prices 3% from 1 January 2025 and up to 2% from 1 April 2026. It blamed input costs and currency swings. Now Audi has announced a rise of up to 2% from January 2027, which reports call its second hike of 2026. Tata Motors has announced its fourth hike of 2026. Hyundai and Audi have blamed rising costs each time.

lesson.concept: How a spending threshold fee works
lesson.big_idea: Some fees switch on only after you cross a set spending line. The key question is whether the fee then hits only the part above the line, or everything.

steps.title: A threshold is a line
steps.text: A threshold is a set amount that changes the rules. Below it, nothing happens. Cross it, and a fee or tax switches on. Lines like this mean people who spend little pay no fee.

steps.title: Two kinds of line
steps.text: A marginal threshold charges only the amount above the line, like income tax slabs. A cliff threshold charges the whole amount once you cross the line. The same 1% rate can cost very different sums under each.

steps.title: SBI Card's fuel rule is a cliff
steps.text: From 1 December, as reported, SBI Card charges 1% on total fuel spend if fuel spends in a billing cycle exceed ₹50,000. A billing cycle is the period between two card statements.

steps.title: Transport counts each payment
steps.text: For transport, the test is each single transaction. As reported, a transport transaction above ₹30,000 attracts a 1% charge. Smaller transport payments do not, however many you make.

steps.title: The count restarts each cycle
steps.text: The fuel total is measured per billing cycle. A heavy month does not carry over, so each new statement period starts again from zero.

example.setup: Say Ravi drives for work and pays for all his fuel with an SBI credit card. He spends ₹48,000 on fuel in one billing cycle and ₹52,000 in the next.

lines.label: Cycle 1 spend
lines.note: The line is not crossed, so the fee stays off.

lines.label: Cycle 1 fee
lines.note: Nothing extra to pay on fuel this cycle.

lines.label: Cycle 2 spend
lines.note: The line is crossed, so the 1% fee switches on.

lines.label: Cycle 2 fee
lines.note: Charged on the whole fuel total, because this is a cliff.

lines.label: If it were marginal
lines.note: Only the part above ₹50,000 would be charged.

lines.label: Cost of the extra fuel
lines.note: The last few thousand rupees became very expensive.

example.result: Crossing the line by just ₹2,000 cost Ravi ₹520, not ₹20. With a cliff threshold, knowing how close you are to the line matters more than the rate itself.

apply.text: So from 1 December, an SBI Card user whose fuel spend creeps just past ₹50,000 in a cycle pays 1% on all of it, as Ravi did. Each transport payment above ₹30,000 also attracts 1%. These details come from a secondary blog, so check SBI Card's own notice.

practice.q: Meera's SBI card fuel spend is ₹50,000 in one billing cycle and ₹60,000 in the next. What fuel fee does she pay each time?
practice.answer: Cycle one: ₹50,000 does not exceed ₹50,000, so the fee is ₹0. Cycle two: ₹60,000 exceeds the line, so 1% applies to the whole total. 1% of ₹60,000 = ₹600. She pays ₹600 in total.

options: No fee, because it is close to ₹50,000

check.why: The fuel rule is a cliff: once spend exceeds ₹50,000, the 1% applies to the total fuel spend, not just the extra.

takeaways: A cliff threshold fee charges everything once you cross the line, not just the extra.

scenes.speak: मान लीजिए Ravi अपना सारा fuel SBI card से भरता है। एक cycle में वो 48000 रुपये खर्च करता है। ये line से नीचे है, तो fee zero। अगली cycle में वो 52000 खर्च करता है। Line पार हो गई, तो अब पूरे amount का 1 percent देना होगा: 520 रुपये।

scenes.say: Ab compare kijiye. Agar rule marginal hota, toh sirf line ke upar ke 2000 par charge lagta: 20 rupaye. Lekin yahan 4000 rupaye ke extra fuel ne Ravi ko 520 rupaye fees mein padwa diye. Yeh extra par lagbhag 13 percent jaisa hai.
scenes.speak: अब compare कीजिए। अगर rule marginal होता, तो सिर्फ line के ऊपर के 2000 पर charge लगता: 20 रुपये। लेकिन यहाँ 4000 रुपये के extra fuel ने Ravi को 520 रुपये fees में पड़वा दिए। ये extra पर लगभग 13 percent जैसा है।

scenes.say: Toh aapke liye iska matlab kya hai? Hyundai lene ka plan hai? 1 December se pehle khareedne par 8000 rupaye tak bach sakte hain. Dealer se poochiye ki kaunsi date price fix karti hai. Agar aap ek cycle mein SBI card par 50000 rupaye se zyada fuel bharte hain, toh fee ke liye taiyaar rahiye. ICICI accounts wale NRIs bhi zyada denge.
scenes.show: Buy before 1 Dec; watch fuel spend
scenes.speak: तो आपके लिए इसका मतलब क्या है? Hyundai लेने का plan है? 1 December से पहले खरीदने पर 8000 रुपये तक बच सकते हैं। Dealer से पूछिए कि कौनसी date price fix करती है। अगर आप एक cycle में SBI card पर 50000 रुपये से ज़्यादा fuel भरते हैं, तो fee के लिए तैयार रहिए। ICICI accounts वाले NRIs भी ज़्यादा देंगे।

scenes.say: Ek aam galti: yeh sochna ki fuel fee sirf 50000 se upar ke kharch par lagti hai. Reports ke mutabik, yeh poore total par lagti hai. Jio 399 users ke liye daily cap nahi hai. Pensioners ko 30 November tak Digital Life Certificate jama karna hai. Aur SBI Card ka apna notice zaroor check kijiye, kyunki yeh details ek secondary blog se aayi hain.
scenes.show: Myth: fee only on the extra
scenes.speak: एक आम गलती: ये सोचना कि fuel fee सिर्फ 50000 से ऊपर के खर्च पर लगती है। Reports के मुताबिक, ये पूरे total पर लगती है। Jio 399 users के लिए daily cap नहीं है। Pensioners को 30 November तक Digital Life Certificate जमा करना है। और SBI Card का अपना notice ज़रूर check कीजिए, क्योंकि ये details एक secondary blog से आई हैं।

scenes.say: Aage kya? Jio ke add-ons 26 November se shuru. Pension certificate 30 November tak. 1 December ko Hyundai hike aur nayi bank fees. Advance tax 15 December tak, aur belated returns 31 December tak. Audi ki baari January 2027 mein.
scenes.speak: आगे क्या? Jio के add-ons 26 November से शुरू। Pension certificate 30 November तक। 1 December को Hyundai hike और नई bank fees। Advance tax 15 December तक, और belated returns 31 December तक। Audi की बारी January 2027 में।

scenes.speak: अब तक पता नहीं: कौनसे Hyundai models पर असर पड़ेगा और कितना, Audi की exact date, और 1 December के LPG, jet fuel और CNG के दाम। Oil companies आम तौर पर पहली तारीख को LPG revise करती हैं। और ये भी साफ नहीं कि Jio का change सिर्फ एक limited New Year offer है या नहीं।

scenes.say: Teen baatein yaad rakhiye. Cliff threshold fee line paar karte hi poore amount par charge karti hai, sirf extra par nahi. 1 December se Hyundai cars 8000 rupaye tak mehngi, aur SBI Card 1 percent fees jodega. Aur 1 December ko LPG, December mein tax dates, aur January mein Audi par nazar rakhiye.
scenes.show: Cross the line, pay on everything
scenes.speak: तीन बातें याद रखिए। Cliff threshold fee line पार करते ही पूरे amount पर charge करती है, सिर्फ extra पर नहीं। 1 December से Hyundai cars 8000 रुपये तक महंगी, और SBI Card 1 percent fees जोड़ेगा। और 1 December को LPG, December में tax dates, और January में Audi पर नज़र रखिए।

quiz.q: If CrowdStrike's share price falls before the deal closes, what happens to what Zscaler holders receive?
options: They still get exactly $260.41 a share in cash
They still get 1.135 CrowdStrike shares each, but those are worth less
The deal is cancelled automatically
quiz.why: The ratio fixes the number of shares, not the dollar amount, so the value moves with CrowdStrike's share price.

quiz.q: Which of the 23 November moves could, if it succeeds, legally force a company to change what it does?
options: The Virginia and Oregon lawsuits, through a court injunction
Guterres's call for a UN AI framework
The American Banker survey of bankers
quiz.why: A court can order an injunction. Guterres's call is not binding, and a survey sets no rules.

quiz.q: Why did SAD win only 1 of 117 seats in 2022 despite getting 18.38% of the vote?
options: Each seat goes to the top vote-getter, and SAD's votes rarely came first in any seat
Seats are handed out in proportion to each party's vote share
Most of SAD's votes were cancelled by the Election Commission
quiz.why: Under first past the post only first place wins a seat, so votes spread thinly across many seats win almost nothing.
